clue.text: Island scientist to tamper with extra gold

parts.note: to doctor something is to falsify or interfere with it
more means additional or extra
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: A researcher on an island fiddles with surplus gold bullion.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points to H. G. Wells's novel The Island of Doctor Moreau, whose title character experiments on animals on a remote island.
explanation.definitionFit: Wells's vivisectionist lives and works on an isolated Pacific island, so he is the island's resident man of science.

clue.text: Heroic exploits in these titles

definitions.meaning: legal documents proving ownership of property, also called title documents

explanation.walkthrough: Property ownership is proved by title documents, so the second definition means those papers.
explanation.definitionFit: Brave feats are noble acts, and legal papers proving ownership of land carry the same name.

clue.text: Literary gourmand's to provide food column

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', so the definition is a literary glutton

parts.note: to cater is to supply food
a pillar is a column

explanation.surface: A bookish glutton is going to supply food for a newspaper column.
explanation.walkthrough: Eric Carle's picture book The Very Hungry Caterpillar follows a creature that eats its way through a huge pile of food.
explanation.definitionFit: Eric Carle's very hungry larva eats its way through a week of food, a glutton from children's literature.

clue.text: Ordinary kiss hasn't disheartened Eleanor, who's completely fine

parts.note: Chambers gives lip as a verb meaning to kiss or touch with the lips

indicators.note: disheartened means the heart, the middle letter, is removed from the word

explanation.surface: Eleanor is fine though nobody has given her even a simple kiss.
explanation.walkthrough: Gail Honeyman's novel Eleanor Oliphant Is Completely Fine supplies the definition. 'disheartened' drops the middle S of HASNT, leaving HANT.
explanation.definitionFit: Gail Honeyman's novel title names its heroine Eleanor and declares her completely fine.

clue.text: Dublin's Molly Bloom finally single

indicators.note: finally takes the closing letter of the word just before it

parts.note: alone means single, on one's own

explanation.surface: Molly Bloom, the Dublin wife in Ulysses, ends up on her own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Molly Bloom' looks like Joyce's heroine, but the name splits: Molly belongs to the definition, the Dublin street-trader of the song 'Molly Malone'.
explanation.definitionFit: Molly Malone is the fishmonger of the ballad that serves as Dublin's unofficial anthem.

clue.text: 40 per cent reduction in farming-related work where machines replace human labour

definitions.text: work where machines replace human labour

indicators.note: forty per cent of a five-letter word is two letters, so the closing two are cut away and the front kept

parts.note: rural means relating to the countryside and farming

explanation.surface: Automation is cutting farm work by almost half.
explanation.walkthrough: Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots) introduced the word robot.
explanation.definitionFit: Čapek's play shows artificial workers built to replace people and is where the term robot began.

clue.text: Story of DeLillo touring Maine with a car

indicators.note: touring suggests wandering about, so the letters travel into a new order

explanation.surface: A novelist's tale of driving around Maine.
explanation.walkthrough: Americana (1971) was Don DeLillo's first novel, about a TV executive's road trip across America.
explanation.definitionFit: DeLillo's debut novel follows a road journey across the country it is named after.

clue.text: First husband's left Chris, who acts as guardian to an Empress

definitions.text: who acts as guardian to an Empress

indicators.note: left means departed, so a letter is taken away from the actor's surname

parts.note: Chris Hemsworth, the Australian actor who plays Thor

indicators.note: first takes only the opening letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A woman's first husband walked out on Chris, protector of an empress.
explanation.walkthrough: In P. G. Wodehouse, Lord Emsworth of Blandings Castle devotes himself to his prize pig, the Empress of Blandings.
explanation.definitionFit: Wodehouse's Lord Emsworth dotes on and guards his champion sow, named the Empress of Blandings.

clue.text: Daily Express coverage is adding colour

indicators.note: coverage suggests the outside of each word, its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A tabloid newspaper's reporting is becoming more colourful.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Express is a British tabloid newspaper; 'adding' and 'is' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Dyes are pigments or stains that give things their colour.

clue.text: Pros conducting review of Artemis

indicators.note: a review looks the material over again and here reworks the letters of Artemis into a new order

explanation.surface: Professionals give their verdict on the Greek goddess Artemis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pros conducting' looks like professionals running something; it means professional conductors of orchestras.
explanation.definitionFit: Maestri is the Italian plural for eminent orchestral conductors, professionals who wield the baton.

clue.text: Theft of Scandi-noir author's style on the radio?

indicators.note: radio is heard rather than read, so what follows is the sound of a phrase

parts.note: Stieg Larsson wrote the Millennium thrillers; something in his manner would jokingly be Larsson-y

explanation.surface: Was the style of a Nordic crime writer stolen, as reported in a broadcast?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the made-up adjective: Larsson-y, 'like Stieg Larsson', said out loud matches the legal word for stealing.
explanation.definitionFit: Larceny is the old legal term for stealing someone's property.

clue.text: Smarter bet is replacing silver

indicators.note: replacing tells us one piece takes the place of another inside the word for a bet

parts.note: a wager is a bet
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
taken as written

explanation.surface: A more clever gambler swaps silver for a different stake.
explanation.definitionFit: Wiser means having better judgment, the same as cleverer or brighter.

clue.text: High-street fashion chain helps oppressed women

parts.note: H&M is a clothing retailer; the ampersand is read out as the word 'and'
aids means helps

explanation.surface: A clothing retailer supports women who are downtrodden.
explanation.walkthrough: H&M is a Swedish clothes chain found on British high streets (main shopping streets). Margaret Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale is about enslaved women.
explanation.definitionFit: In Atwood's Gilead the handmaids are women forced into servitude and childbearing, the novel's emblem of subjugation.

clue.text: Spark novel reminder of death in some men (Tom or Ian)

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit within the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A novel tells of death haunting a group of men, named Tom or Ian.
explanation.walkthrough: The run of letters spans 'soME MEN TOM OR Ian'. Muriel Spark's 1959 novel shares its title with the Latin phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Muriel Spark's novel takes its name from the Latin phrase for an object that warns its owner of mortality.

clue.text: Older star's concerning dating arrangement

parts.note: re is a short word meaning about or concerning

indicators.note: an arrangement sets things out in a different order, so the letters of dating are shuffled

explanation.surface: An ageing celebrity discusses the details of a romantic date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Older star' suggests an ageing celebrity; it is an astronomical star late in its life.
explanation.definitionFit: A red giant is a star in a late stage of its life, swollen after its core hydrogen runs out.

parts.note: a poem is one example of a literary work
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Day Lewis' looks like the poet Cecil Day-Lewis; the name splits into DAY and the last letter of Lewis's.
explanation.definitionFit: Commuters travel on the working days of the week, Monday to Friday.

clue.text: By no means the essential part of Dylan Thomas comprehended

indicators.note: comprehended in its old sense of took in or enclosed, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: Thomas Hardy, the novelist and poet

indicators.note: the essential part of a word is its centre, the single middle letter of the name Dylan

explanation.surface: Not really grasping the core of Dylan Thomas's poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dylan Thomas' reads as one poet, but it splits: the middle of Dylan, and a different Thomas, the novelist Hardy.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardly and by no means both say scarcely at all, used to deny something.

clue.text: First covers released, including new one in range

indicators.note: covers means the word for first goes around what follows

parts.note: main means chief or first in importance

indicators.note: including means the word for released has another letter put inside it

parts.note: out means freed or released

explanation.surface: The first book jackets released include a new one about a mountain range.
explanation.definitionFit: A range is a chain of peaks, so each single peak is one member of it.

clue.text: Almost fall over, beginning to lean towards each other

indicators.note: over in a down clue means the piece is turned upside down, read from the bottom
almost means the word is not quite complete, losing its final letter

parts.note: fall is the American word for autumn

indicators.note: beginning to takes only the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: Nearly toppling, two people start to lean in to each other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' cuts AUTUMN to AUTUM; 'over' turns it to MUTUA.
explanation.definitionFit: Mutual feelings run both ways, shared by two people and directed at one another.

clue.text: Outlaw cakes and sweets following unhealthy food expert's announcement

indicators.note: following places the cakes and sweets after the food expert in the answer

parts.note: a fryer cooks fried food, the unhealthy kind
tuck is British schoolchildren's slang for snacks such as cakes and sweets

explanation.surface: A criminal says he serves sweets and cakes after a junk-food specialist speaks.
explanation.walkthrough: Friar Tuck is the jovial monk among Robin Hood's band of outlaws.
explanation.definitionFit: Friar Tuck is one of Robin Hood's Merry Men, a band of outlaws in Sherwood Forest.

clue.text: Feel aching, exhausted?

indicators.note: exhausted here means emptied, so each word keeps only its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone sore and worn out asks whether they are spent.
explanation.walkthrough: Emptying 'Feel' leaves FL and emptying 'aching' leaves AG; the whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To flag is to tire or droop, which is how a sore and worn-out person feels.

clue.text: Her hero's disguised in Zorro's mask, cry out

indicators.note: out means put out of order, so the letters are rearranged
a mask covers the outside of a face, so only the first and last letters of the name are used

explanation.surface: A heroine cries out on seeing her masked hero Zorro.
explanation.walkthrough: Baroness Orczy wrote The Scarlet Pimpernel, whose hero hides behind the disguise of a foppish aristocrat. 'mask' gives ZO, which joins CRY to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Orczy created Sir Percy Blakeney, a hero who works in disguise as the Scarlet Pimpernel.

clue.text: Bluff has taken in one player in Casino Royale

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bluff' and 'player' suggest poker; the bluff is a cliff, and the player is the actor Daniel Craig, Bond in the 2006 film.
explanation.definitionFit: Daniel Craig played James Bond in the film Casino Royale, so he is one of its actors.
